lessons.title: Counting 1–10
lessons.subject: Math
lessons.reading_material: Numbers are all around us! When you count apples in a basket or steps up the stairs, you use numbers. The numbers 1 to 10 are the building blocks of all mathematics. Let's learn them together! Each number represents a specific quantity: 1 is one object, 2 is two objects, and so on up to 10.
practical_activities: Count classroom objects (books, pencils, chairs)
Play the 'how many fingers' game
Draw dots to match numbers on a number line
Use coloured counters to show each number

exercises.q: How many fingers do you have on one hand?
Write the number that comes after 7.

homework.task: Count 5 different objects at home and draw them in your book.

revision.notes: Numbers 1–10 are used to count. Each number is exactly 1 more than the previous.
revision.tip: Review this lesson before the next class

lessons.title: Counting 11–20
lessons.subject: Math
learning_objectives: Understand teen numbers as 10 + some ones
lessons.reading_material: After learning 1–10, we extend to 11–20. Teen numbers are special: they are all made of one group of ten plus some extra ones. 11 is ten and one more, 12 is ten and two more, and so on. Understanding this helps prepare you for place value!
practical_activities: Use ten-frames to show teen numbers
Build numbers with base-ten blocks
Count classroom items arranged in groups of ten

exercises.q: Write the number that comes after 14.

homework.task: Count all the steps in your home. Write the number.

revision.notes: Teen numbers: 11=10+1, 12=10+2 … 20=10+10. Ten is a key building block.
revision.tip: Review this lesson before the next class

lessons.title: Addition to 10
lessons.subject: Math
learning_objectives: Add two numbers with a sum up to 10
lessons.reading_material: Addition means putting groups together to find the total. When you have 3 apples and someone gives you 2 more, you add: 3 + 2 = 5. The '+' symbol means 'add' or 'plus'. The '=' symbol means 'equals' or 'is the same as'.
practical_activities: Use counters: put 4 red and 3 blue together, count total
Draw pictures to show addition stories
Play 'addition war' card game

homework.task: Make up 5 addition stories using toys or snacks at home.

revision.notes: Addition: combining two groups. 2 + 3 = 5. Order doesn't matter: 2+3 = 3+2.
revision.tip: Review this lesson before the next class

lessons.title: Subtraction to 10
lessons.subject: Math
lessons.reading_material: Subtraction means taking away from a group. If you have 8 cookies and eat 3, you have 8 − 3 = 5 left. The '−' symbol means 'subtract' or 'minus'. Subtraction is the opposite of addition.
practical_activities: Act out subtraction stories with classroom objects
Use a number line to count back
Draw crossing-out pictures

homework.task: Count 10 blocks. Take some away. Write the subtraction sentence.

revision.notes: Subtraction: 8 − 3 = 5. Count back on a number line. Check: 5 + 3 = 8.
revision.tip: Review this lesson before the next class

lessons.title: Shapes and Patterns
lessons.subject: Math
lessons.reading_material: Shapes are everywhere! A circle is perfectly round. A square has 4 equal sides and 4 corners. A triangle has 3 sides and 3 corners. A rectangle has 4 sides and 4 corners (opposite sides are equal). Patterns repeat in a regular order — like circle, square, circle, square.
practical_activities: Shape hunt around the classroom
Sort objects by shape
Create AB and ABC patterns with coloured tiles

exercises.q: How many sides does a triangle have?

homework.task: Find 3 examples of each shape at home and draw them.

revision.notes: Circle=0 sides, Triangle=3 sides, Square=4 equal sides, Rectangle=4 sides.
revision.tip: Review this lesson before the next class

questions.q: How many corners does a square have?

lessons.title: Measurement: Length and Weight
lessons.subject: Math
lessons.reading_material: Measurement helps us describe the world. Length tells us how long something is. We can compare: a pencil is longer than a crayon. Weight tells us how heavy something is. We can compare: a book is heavier than a feather. Before rulers and scales, people used hands, feet, and other objects to measure.
practical_activities: Measure objects using cubes or paper clips
Compare two objects by weighing in your hands
Order 3 objects from shortest to longest

exercises.q: Which is longer: a pencil or a paper clip?
Order: book, eraser, ruler from shortest to longest.

homework.task: Measure 5 objects at home using your hand spans. Record results.

revision.notes: Compare lengths and weights by direct comparison. Use non-standard units for measuring.
revision.tip: Review this lesson before the next class

questions.q: A cat is ___ than an ant.
How many paper clips long is a pencil if it takes 8?

lessons.title: Time: Days and Seasons
lessons.subject: Math
learning_objectives: Name days of the week in order
lessons.reading_material: Time helps us organise our day. There are 7 days in a week: Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday, Friday, Saturday, Sunday. Each day has parts: morning (when you wake up), afternoon (after lunch), evening (before dinner), and night (when you sleep). The year has four seasons: Spring, Summer, Autumn, Winter.
practical_activities: Make a weekly calendar
Act out daily routines
Match activities to times of day

exercises.q: Name the season when leaves fall off trees.

homework.task: Write what you do in the morning, afternoon, and evening tomorrow.

revision.notes: Days: Mon, Tue, Wed, Thu, Fri, Sat, Sun. Seasons: Spring, Summer, Autumn, Winter.
revision.tip: Review this lesson before the next class

questions.q: How many days are in a week?

lessons.title: Data: Sorting and Graphing
lessons.subject: Math
lessons.reading_material: Data is information we collect. We can sort things by colour, shape, or size. A picture graph shows data using pictures. If we survey the class about favourite fruit: 5 students like apples, 3 like bananas, 4 like oranges. We can show this in a picture graph!
practical_activities: Sort coloured buttons by colour
Create a favourite colour class survey
Draw a picture graph from survey results

exercises.q: 3 students like cats and 5 like dogs. How many altogether?

homework.task: Survey 5 family members: cat or dog? Draw a picture graph.

revision.notes: Sort by attributes. Picture graphs use pictures to show data. Read: most, least, total.
revision.tip: Review this lesson before the next class

lessons.title: Phonics: Alphabet and Letter Sounds
lessons.subject: English
learning_objectives: Recognise all 26 letters of the alphabet
Produce the sound for each letter
lessons.reading_material: The alphabet has 26 letters — 5 vowels (a, e, i, o, u) and 21 consonants. Each letter has a name and a SOUND. The letter 'b' is called 'bee' but says /b/ as in 'ball'. When we blend letter sounds together, we make words. CVC words: Consonant-Vowel-Consonant, like c-a-t → 'cat'. Phonics is the key to reading!
practical_activities: Alphabet chant and action song
Sound sort with picture cards
Build CVC words with letter tiles

homework.task: Write the letter that starts each picture: apple, boat, cat, dog, egg.

revision.notes: 26 letters: 5 vowels (a,e,i,o,u), 21 consonants. CVC blending: say each sound fast → word.
revision.tip: Review this lesson before the next class

lessons.title: Sight Words and Simple Sentences
lessons.subject: English
learning_objectives: Understand capital letters and full stops
lessons.reading_material: SIGHT WORDS are common words we learn to recognise instantly without sounding out: the, a, is, it, in, on, am, I, we, he, she, they, was, are, to, do, you, your. Learning sight words helps you read fluently! A SENTENCE is a group of words that makes complete sense. It starts with a CAPITAL LETTER and ends with a FULL STOP.
practical_activities: Sight word flash cards
Build sentences with word cards
Reading simple decodable books

exercises.q: Correct this sentence: the cat sat on mat
exercises.answer: The cat sat on the mat.

homework.task: Write 5 sentences using sight words. Draw a picture for each.

revision.notes: Sight words: memorise by sight. Sentence: starts capital, ends full stop, makes sense.
revision.tip: Review this lesson before the next class

questions.q: What does a sentence end with?
Is this a sentence? 'running fast dog'

lessons.title: Reading: Simple Stories
lessons.subject: English
lessons.reading_material: Reading is the most important skill you will learn! Good readers: look at pictures for clues, sound out new words, re-read if confused, think about the meaning. When we understand what we read, we call it COMPREHENSION. After reading a story, we can answer WHO (characters), WHERE (setting), and WHAT (events) questions.
practical_activities: Read aloud with expression
Hot seat character questions
Story sequence cards

exercises.q: What do we call the people in a story?
After reading 'The Three Bears', who sat in the smallest chair?

homework.task: Read a short book. Draw and write: Who is in the story? Where does it happen? What happens?

revision.notes: Comprehension: WHO (characters), WHERE (setting), WHAT (events), WHY (reasons). Retell in order: beginning, middle, end.
revision.tip: Review this lesson before the next class

lessons.title: Writing: Simple Sentences and Descriptions
lessons.subject: English
lessons.reading_material: Writing lets us share our ideas! Good writing uses DESCRIBING WORDS (adjectives) to paint a picture. Instead of 'I have a cat', try 'I have a fluffy, brown cat'. Adjectives make writing more interesting. When we write, we think BEFORE we write (plan), write our ideas, and then CHECK our work.
practical_activities: Label pictures with adjectives
Write about favourite animal with describing words
Illustrated class book creation

exercises.q: Add two adjectives: 'I have a ___ ___ dog.'

homework.task: Write 3 sentences about your favourite food. Use at least one adjective in each.

revision.notes: Adjectives describe nouns. Good writing: plan → write → check. Use capital and full stop for each sentence.
revision.tip: Review this lesson before the next class

lessons.title: Grammar: Nouns and Verbs
lessons.subject: English
learning_objectives: Sort words into nouns and verbs
lessons.reading_material: Every sentence has NOUNS and VERBS. A NOUN is a naming word — it names a person (girl, teacher), place (school, park), thing (book, pencil), or animal (cat, bird). A VERB is a doing or action word — it tells us what happens (run, eat, play, jump, think). 'The girl reads a book.' — girl=noun, reads=verb, book=noun.
practical_activities: Noun hunt around the classroom
Action mime then write the verb
Sort word cards into nouns and verbs

exercises.q: Find the verb: 'The dog runs fast.'

homework.task: Write 5 nouns you can see and 5 verbs you can do. Use each in a sentence.

revision.notes: Noun=naming word (person/place/thing/animal). Verb=action word (doing/being). Every sentence needs both.
revision.tip: Review this lesson before the next class

questions.q: 'The bird sings' — what is the verb?

lessons.title: Poetry: Rhyme and Rhythm
lessons.subject: English
learning_objectives: Clap the rhythm of a poem
lessons.reading_material: Poetry is a special type of writing that plays with words, sound, and rhythm. RHYMING words end with the same sound: cat/hat/mat, fun/sun/run. The RHYTHM of a poem is its beat — we can clap it! Many nursery rhymes have patterns. A COUPLET is two rhyming lines together. Poetry doesn't have to rhyme, but rhyme makes it fun to say aloud!
practical_activities: Rhyme sorting game
Clap rhythm of favourite nursery rhymes
Write class rhyming poem

exercises.q: Complete: 'I see a cat / sitting on a ___'

homework.task: Write a poem with 4 lines. Lines 1&2 rhyme, lines 3&4 rhyme. Draw a picture.

revision.notes: Rhyme: same ending sound. Couplet: two rhyming lines. Rhythm: the beat. Read aloud to feel it.
revision.tip: Review this lesson before the next class

lessons.title: Living and Non-Living Things
lessons.subject: Science
lessons.reading_material: Everything around us is either living or non-living. Living things breathe, grow, eat, and reproduce. Plants and animals are living things. Rocks, chairs, and water are non-living.
practical_activities: Sort classroom objects into living/non-living
Draw one living and one non-living thing

homework.task: Find 3 living and 3 non-living things at home

revision.notes: Living things need food, water, air; non-living things do not.
revision.tip: Review this lesson before the next class

lessons.title: Parts of a Plant
lessons.subject: Science
learning_objectives: Name the main parts of a plant
lessons.reading_material: Plants have roots, stem, leaves, and flowers. Roots absorb water. The stem carries water to leaves. Leaves make food using sunlight. Flowers produce seeds.
practical_activities: Label a plant diagram
Plant a seed and observe over a week

homework.task: Draw and label a plant

revision.notes: Remember: roots → stem → leaves → flower → seed is the order.
revision.tip: Review this lesson before the next class

lessons.title: Animals and Their Habitats
lessons.subject: Science
lessons.reading_material: Different animals live in different places called habitats. Fish live in water. Birds live in trees. Lions live on grasslands. Each animal is suited to its habitat.
practical_activities: Match animal cards to habitat pictures
Act out being an animal in its habitat

homework.task: Draw your favourite animal and its habitat

revision.notes: Habitat provides food, shelter, and water for an animal.
revision.tip: Review this lesson before the next class

lessons.title: Stories from Around the World
lessons.subject: World Literature
learning_objectives: Listen to and retell a story from another culture
lessons.reading_material: Stories have been told in every culture for thousands of years. 'Cinderella' exists in over 500 versions worldwide. In China it is called Yeh-Shen. In Egypt, the earliest version is 'Rhodopis'. Japanese fairy tales include 'Momotaro' (the Peach Boy), a brave boy who fights demons. African folktales often feature clever animals like Anansi the Spider. Stories help us understand other cultures and share universal values like kindness and courage.
practical_activities: Story circle: take turns adding one sentence to a collaborative world story
exercises: Name a folktale from 3 different countries
lessons.homework: Draw your favourite moment from a folktale and write one sentence about it.

revision.notes: Folktales share universal themes across cultures. Anansi = African trickster spider. Momotaro = Japanese peach boy.
revision.tip: Draw pictures to remember story characters.

info_cards.title: Famous Photograph: Earthrise
info_cards.fact: "Earthrise" is a famous photograph, credited to NASA / William Anders, Apollo 8.

info_cards.title: Famous Painting: Mona Lisa
info_cards.fact: "Mona Lisa" by Leonardo da Vinci. Famous for its subject's mysterious smile, it hangs in the Louvre Museum in Paris.

info_cards.title: Famous Painting: The Starry Night
info_cards.fact: "The Starry Night" by Vincent van Gogh. Painted in 1889, it shows a swirling night sky over a quiet village.

info_cards.title: Famous Painting: Sunflowers
info_cards.fact: "Sunflowers" by Vincent van Gogh. Van Gogh painted several versions of sunflowers in a vase using bright yellow paint.

info_cards.title: Famous Painting: Girl with a Pearl Earring
info_cards.fact: "Girl with a Pearl Earring" by Johannes Vermeer. A 17th-century Dutch portrait nicknamed the 'Mona Lisa of the North'.

info_cards.title: Famous Painting: The Great Wave off Kanagawa
info_cards.fact: "The Great Wave off Kanagawa" by Katsushika Hokusai. A famous Japanese woodblock print showing a huge wave near Mount Fuji.

info_cards.title: Famous Painting: The Hay Wain
info_cards.fact: "The Hay Wain" by John Constable. An English countryside scene showing a horse-drawn cart crossing a river.

info_cards.title: Famous Painting: The Night Watch
info_cards.fact: "The Night Watch" by Rembrandt. A large group portrait of a militia company, known for its dramatic light and shadow.

info_cards.title: Famous Painting: The Persistence of Memory
info_cards.fact: "The Persistence of Memory" by Salvador Dali. A surrealist painting famous for its melting clocks in a desert landscape.

info_cards.title: Famous Painting: The Scream
info_cards.fact: "The Scream" by Edvard Munch. A Norwegian painting showing a figure with an agonized expression against a swirling sky.

info_cards.title: Famous Painting: Water Lilies
info_cards.fact: "Water Lilies" by Claude Monet. Part of a series of about 250 paintings Monet made of his garden pond in Giverny, France.

info_cards.title: Famous Sculpture: Christ the Redeemer
info_cards.fact: "Christ the Redeemer" by Paul Landowski. A giant statue overlooking Rio de Janeiro, Brazil, completed in 1931.

info_cards.title: Famous Sculpture: Mount Rushmore
info_cards.fact: "Mount Rushmore" by Gutzon Borglum. Carved into a mountain in South Dakota, it shows the faces of four U.S. presidents.

info_cards.title: Famous Sculpture: Statue of Liberty
info_cards.fact: "Statue of Liberty" by Frederic Auguste Bartholdi. A gift from France to the United States, standing in New York Harbor since 1886.

info_cards.title: Famous Sculpture: The Great Sphinx of Giza
info_cards.fact: "The Great Sphinx of Giza" by Ancient Egyptian sculptors. A huge limestone statue with a lion's body and a human head, built thousands of years ago.

info_cards.title: Famous Sculpture: The Lincoln Memorial statue
info_cards.fact: "The Lincoln Memorial statue" by Daniel Chester French. A large seated statue of President Abraham Lincoln in Washington, D.C.

info_cards.title: Famous Sculpture: The Moai of Easter Island
info_cards.fact: "The Moai of Easter Island" by Rapa Nui people. Hundreds of giant stone head statues carved centuries ago on a remote Pacific island.

info_cards.title: Famous Sculpture: The Terracotta Army
info_cards.fact: "The Terracotta Army" by Craftsmen of Qin Shi Huang. Thousands of life-sized clay soldier statues buried to guard an ancient Chinese emperor's tomb.

info_cards.title: Famous Sculpture: Winged Victory of Samothrace
info_cards.fact: "Winged Victory of Samothrace" by Unknown ancient Greek sculptor. An ancient marble statue of the goddess Nike, now in the Louvre Museum.

info_cards.title: Famous Sculpture: The Little Mermaid (Copenhagen)
info_cards.fact: "The Little Mermaid (Copenhagen)" by Edvard Eriksen. A bronze statue sitting on a rock in Copenhagen's harbour, inspired by Hans Christian Andersen's tale.

info_cards.title: Famous Sculpture: Manneken Pis
info_cards.fact: "Manneken Pis" by Jerome Duquesnoy. A small, famous bronze fountain statue of a boy in Brussels, Belgium.

info_cards.title: Famous Quote
info_cards.fact: "Be yourself; everyone else is already taken." — Oscar Wilde, Irish writer.

info_cards.title: Famous Person: Marie Curie
info_cards.fact: Marie Curie was a scientist who discovered the elements polonium and radium, and won Nobel Prizes in both Physics and Chemistry.

info_cards.title: Book Summary: Silent Spring
info_cards.fact: "Silent Spring" by Rachel Carson (1962) is a non-fiction book that warned about the harm pesticides like DDT cause to birds and the environment, helping start the modern environmental movement.

info_cards.title: Book Summary: Cosmos
info_cards.fact: "Cosmos" by Carl Sagan explores the universe, the history of science, and our place among the stars.

info_cards.title: Notable Person: Helen Keller
info_cards.fact: "Alone we can do so little; together we can do so much." — American author and disability-rights advocate who, though deaf and blind from infancy, learned to read, write, and speak.

info_cards.title: Notable Person: Martin Luther King Jr.
info_cards.fact: "I have a dream that my four little children will one day live in a nation where they will not be judged by the color of their skin but by the content of their character." — American minister and civil-rights leader who led the 1963 March on Washington.

info_cards.title: Notable Person: Rosa Parks
info_cards.fact: "I would like to be remembered as a person who wanted to be free... so other people would also be free." — American civil-rights activist whose refusal to give up her bus seat in 1955 helped spark the Montgomery Bus Boycott.

info_cards.title: Notable Person: Mahatma Gandhi
info_cards.fact: "Be the change that you wish to see in the world." — Indian lawyer and independence leader who led India's nonviolent struggle for freedom from British rule.

info_cards.title: Notable Person: Walt Disney
info_cards.fact: "If you can dream it, you can do it." — American animator and entrepreneur who created Mickey Mouse and founded the Walt Disney Company.

info_cards.title: Notable Person: Wilbur Wright
info_cards.fact: "It is possible to fly without motors, but not without knowledge and skill." — American inventor who, with his brother Orville, built and flew the first successful powered airplane in 1903.

info_cards.title: Notable Person: Orville Wright
info_cards.fact: "The desire to fly is an idea handed down to us by our ancestors." — American inventor who, with his brother Wilbur, achieved the first powered, controlled airplane flight in 1903.

info_cards.title: Notable Person: Mother Teresa
info_cards.fact: "Spread love everywhere you go." — Catholic nun and missionary who founded the Missionaries of Charity to help the poor and sick in Kolkata, India.

info_cards.title: Notable Person: Florence Nightingale
info_cards.fact: "I attribute my success to this: I never gave or took an excuse." — British nurse known as the founder of modern nursing for her work improving hospital care during the Crimean War.

info_cards.title: Notable Person: Jane Goodall
info_cards.fact: "What you do makes a difference, and you have to decide what kind of difference you want to make." — British primatologist famous for her decades of research on wild chimpanzees in Tanzania.

info_cards.title: Notable Person: Neil Armstrong
info_cards.fact: "That's one small step for man, one giant leap for mankind." — American astronaut who became the first person to walk on the Moon in 1969.

info_cards.title: Notable Person: Amelia Earhart
info_cards.fact: "The most effective way to do it is to do it." — American aviator who became the first woman to fly solo across the Atlantic Ocean.

info_cards.title: Notable Person: Fred Rogers
info_cards.fact: "There are three ways to ultimate success: the first way is to be kind, the second way is to be kind, the third way is to be kind." — American television host who created and hosted the children's show Mister Rogers' Neighborhood.

info_cards.title: Notable Person: Maya Angelou
info_cards.fact: "Try to be a rainbow in someone's cloud." — American poet and author best known for her memoir I Know Why the Caged Bird Sings.

info_cards.title: Notable Person: Jim Henson
info_cards.fact: "Kids don't remember what you try to teach them. They remember what you are." — American puppeteer who created the Muppets, including Kermit the Frog and Sesame Street's characters.

info_cards.title: Notable Person: Dr. Seuss (Theodor Geisel)
info_cards.fact: "Oh, the places you'll go!" — American children's author and illustrator who wrote The Cat in the Hat and Green Eggs and Ham.

info_cards.title: Notable Person: Jacques Cousteau
info_cards.fact: "The sea, once it casts its spell, holds one in its net of wonder forever." — French explorer and filmmaker who pioneered ocean exploration and underwater documentary filmmaking.

info_cards.title: Notable Person: Anne Sullivan
info_cards.fact: "Knowledge is love and light and vision." — American teacher best known for educating Helen Keller, who was both deaf and blind.

info_cards.title: Notable Person: Louis Braille
info_cards.fact: "Access to communication in the widest sense is access to knowledge." — French educator who, blind himself from childhood, invented the Braille reading and writing system for the blind.

info_cards.title: Notable Person: Benjamin Franklin
info_cards.fact: "An investment in knowledge pays the best interest." — American statesman, inventor, and writer who helped draft the U.S. Declaration of Independence.

learning_objectives: Identify common animals and their homes
lessons.reading_material: Our world is a wonderful place! There are 7 continents: Africa, Asia, Europe, North America, South America, Australia, and Antarctica. There are 5 oceans: Pacific, Atlantic, Indian, Southern, and Arctic. Animals live in different habitats — lions in grasslands, penguins in Antarctica, fish in oceans. The Sun gives us light and warmth; the Moon lights the night sky.
practical_activities: Point to continents on a globe; match animal flashcards to their habitats
lessons.homework: Draw a world map and colour the 7 continents in different colours.

revision.notes: 7 continents, 5 oceans. Animals live in habitats that suit them.
revision.tip: Use a song or rhyme to remember the 7 continents.

lessons.assessment: Name 3 continents and one animal from each.

lessons.title: My Family and Community
lessons.subject: Social Studies
lessons.reading_material: A family is a group of people who love and care for each other. Families can be big or small. A community is the group of people who live near each other and share places like schools, parks, and shops. Community helpers — doctors, teachers, police officers, and firefighters — keep our community safe and healthy. Everyone in the community has a role to play.

revision.notes: Family = people who care for each other. Community = people sharing the same area.
revision.tip: Think about what helpers in your community do for YOU.
